title: Bridged on-call runbook and status templates
author: Carlos Rivera
body:
Overview

Purpose
This runbook documents the bridged on-call model used by Redwood Inference for multi-team incident coordination, the incident lifecycle from detection to RCA, and a set of ready-to-send status page and customer communication templates. It is intended for SREs, service owners, on-call engineers, and product incident leads.

Scope
- Applies to all production service incidents affecting latency, availability, throughput, or data integrity for Redwood hosted, dedicated, and private deployments.
- Includes cross-region incidents and cases where a single user-facing outage requires a coordinated bridge.

When to use this document
- When an alert escalates beyond a single responder and a coordinated bridge is required.
- For game-day rehearsals and on-call orientation.

Key roles and responsibilities
- Bridge Lead (BL): runs the incident bridge, keeps notes, coordinates comms. Primary responsibility: accelerate decision-making.
- Primary Responder (PR): first on-call engineer owning the alerting service (e.g., runtime-api).
- Service Owner (SO): product/feature owner for the failing service; provides domain knowledge and approves rollouts.
- SRE Responder (SRE): supports mitigation, rollback, and capacity actions.
- Customer Liaison (CL): crafts customer-facing updates for commercial accounts and support.
- Incident Commander (IC) [when incident > P1 60+ minutes]: oversees post-triage strategy and stakeholder escalation.

Bridge activation criteria (quick checklist)
1. Any outage with customer-visible errors for > 2 minutes.
2. SLO degradation > 3x breach window (e.g., sustained p99 latency above target for 5 minutes).
3. Repeated auto-scaling failures or control-plane errors that block recovery.
4. Anything requiring cross-team coordination (networking, infra, runtime, product).

Quick-start activation steps (first 10 minutes)
1. PR acknowledges alert and confirms impact in monitoring (Datadog/Prometheus).
2. PR posts a short note in #incidents (Slack) and triggers bridge. Use /bridge create runtime-<service> <severity>.
3. BL joins, opens the incident doc (link), and captures: impact, start time, initial hypothesis, and current mitigation attempts.
4. Assign roles: BL, PR, SO, SRE, CL. Record in the bridge header.
5. Send initial status to internal stakeholders (template below).

Incident lifecycle and decision ladder
1. Detection & Validation
   - Validate signal sources (metrics, customer reports, error logs).
   - Check for correlated alerts (region, model-router, kv-cache).
2. Triage & Containment (10–30 minutes)
   - Determine scope: region(s), routes, tenants impacted.
   - If partial, apply traffic rules (route-manager) to reduce blast radius.
   - If noisy or cascading, enable autoscaling-friendly throttles.
3. Mitigation & Stabilization (30–120 minutes)
   - Apply fixes that reduce immediate customer impact: scale up pools, restart pods on affected node pools, clear KV cache entries selectively.
   - Prefer safe rollbacks or config changes over risky code patches.
4. Recovery & Verification (60–240 minutes)
   - Gradually re-enable traffic to affected routes.
   - Confirm SLO metrics returning to baseline; verify end-to-end user flows.
5. Post-Incident (RCA/Rapid Postmortem)
   - BL/IC ensure a postmortem is owned within 48 hours.
   - Postmortems must include timeline, root cause(s), corrective actions, owners, and target completion dates.

Alerting thresholds (examples)
| SLO | Monitoring threshold | Pager threshold | Notes |
|-----|---------------------:|----------------:|-------|
| API availability (hosted) | < 99.9% over 10m | Pager if < 99.5% for 5m | P1 for customer-visible downtime |
| P95 latency (generate) | > 150 ms | Pager if > 300ms for 5m | Adjust per model family |
| Error rate (5xx) | > 0.2% | Pager if > 1% for 3m or exponential increase | Service-specific baselines apply |
| KV cache misses | > 20% change vs baseline | Alert (no page) | Investigate cache invalidation flows |

Service-specific runbook snippets (copy/paste)
- runtime-api (common commands):
```
# Check pods and restarts
kubectl -n prod get pods -l app=runtime-api -o wide
kubectl -n prod logs -l app=runtime-api --since=10m | jq '.message' | grep ERROR

# Force restart a pod set (safe rolling)
kubectl -n prod rollout restart deploy/runtime-api --timeout=10m
```
- route-manager (traffic control):
```
# Temporarily disable route to region-eu-1
routectl set-weight --service runtime-api --route region-eu-1 --weight 0
# Re-enable at safe cadence
routectl set-weight --service runtime-api --route region-eu-1 --weight 50
```

Escalation matrix (time-based)
1. Pager fired -> PR (1 min to respond).
2. No resolution after 15 minutes -> BL + SO join.
3. No effective mitigation after 45 minutes -> IC engages, executive notifs prepared.
4. 120+ minutes with customer impact -> formal incident conference (exec + legal + sales).

Customer and public status templates
- Internal short status (Slack #incidents):
"""
[INC-<id>] runtime-api — Degraded: Increased 5xx rates for hosted API. Impact: ~8% of requests failing, regions: us-west. Start: 2026-02-18T14:02Z. BL: @carlos. Next update in 15 minutes."
"""

- Status page initial (public):
Subject: "Degraded service: Hosted API (generations) — Ongoing"
Body for status page system:
"At 14:02 UTC we identified increased error rates affecting the hosted generation API. Engineers are investigating. Customers may experience timeouts or 5xx errors when calling text generation endpoints in us-west. We will provide an update within 15 minutes. Impact: partial. Affected: hosted API."

- Customer-facing commercial template (for account teams):
Subject: "Redwood Incident: Intermittent errors for hosted API — <short id>"
Body:
"Hello <Customer>,

We are investigating an issue causing intermittent 5xx errors against the hosted generation API impacting requests routed to the us-west region. Our SREs have established an incident bridge and are actively working on mitigation steps. Current mitigation: diverting new traffic from us-west to us-east where possible; no data loss reported.

Estimated time to next update: 15 minutes.

If you have critical production traffic, please reply and we will prioritize a direct bridge.

Owner: Carlos Rivera, SRE & Incident Lead
"

Template for resolution notice (public & customers)
Subject: "Service restored — Hosted API generation — Incident <id>"
Body:
"At 14:47 UTC engineers resolved the issue causing elevated 5xx rates for the hosted generation API. The root cause was a mis-synchronized cache invalidation rolling out with a model routing change. Normal traffic levels have resumed and we are monitoring for regressions. No customer data was affected.

Follow-ups: A post-incident report will be published in 48 hours with remediation steps.

We apologize for the disruption.
"

Postmortem & corrective action standard
- Timeline: initial draft within 48 hours; final RCA published within 7 calendar days.
- Required sections: Summary, Impact, Detection timeline (minute-granular), Root cause analysis, Contributing factors, Short-term mitigations, Long-term fixes, Owners, Verification plan, Lessons learned.
- Severity classification rules: P1 (customer downtime or data loss), P2 (partial degradation of critical flows), P3 (degraded non-critical functions).

Postmortem checklist (owners)
1. Add timeline and logs offsets (BL).
2. Attach monitoring dashboards and traces (SRE).
3. Write and assign corrective actions with due dates (SO).
4. Review with stakeholders, include customer liaison comments (CL).
5. Closure: confirm verification runs and merge related fixes (SRE).

Game day plan (quarterly exercises)
- Frequency: minimum once per quarter; large multi-team exercise annually.
- Objectives: validate bridge process, test runbook actions (route-manager, rollout restart), and exercise customer comms.
- Typical scenario: simulated multi-region latency with a model-router misconfiguration.
- Roles in exercise: designate an observer, a realtime notes taker, and at least one customer-liaison actor.

Game day quick schedule (90 minutes)
0–15m: Inject alert, PR validates, bridge created.
15–45m: Triage & containment, try first mitigation (route weight).
45–75m: Implement full recovery plan (rollback / restart), confirm healthy.
75–90m: Retro and action items captured.

Runbook governance and maintenance
- Ownership: service owners must review runbooks quarterly and after any P1/P2.
- Runbook PRs: stored in the runbooks repo and linked from this page. Major changes require an SRE reviewer.
- Retirement: deprecated runbooks are archived with reason and effective date.

Appendix: quick reference cheat sheet
- Pager priorities: P1 = page all oncall -> escalate to IC after 45m.
- Bridge URL pattern: https://bridge.redwood.ai/incidents/<INC-ID>
- Slack channels: #incidents (public), #incidents-paid (customer-facing), #oncall-sre (internal).
- Key dashboards: runtime-api-slo, route-manager-traffic, kv-cache-hits.

Example verification commands
```
# Check p95 latency from observability
curl -s "https://metrics-api.internal/query?metric=runtime_api_p95&window=5m" | jq .value
# Confirm no recent restarts
kubectl -n prod get pods -l app=runtime-api -o jsonpath='{.items[*].status.containerStatuses[*].restartCount}'
```

Notes and references
- For complex incidents involving customer data or legal impact, include Legal and Security (security@redwood.ai) within 30 minutes.
- Link to configuration playbooks: /confluence/eng-platform/dashboards-and-alerts/runbook-library
